rv.q: The original ”Adventures of Tom Sawyer” is fundamentally a children’s story, but it is a story viewed from the distance of adulthood by a sly and skeptical adult. In their new musical version of the novel, Ken Ludwig and Don Schlitz mean, I think, to honor this split personality.

sg.ra: Minskoff's stage is unusually high, so Row A-B forces you to look almost straight up and you end up staring at performer bodies rather than the elaborate mask and headpiece work the production is designed around; multiple forum regulars describe missing the full effect of the processional costumes from these rows and recommend moving back to at least Row 5.

sg.vl: Aisle is the move for Circle of Life
sg.ra: The Lion King runs its Act I and Act II processional parades down both orchestra aisles, so aisle seats between Rows C and M put you inches from the giraffes, elephant and Young Simba's post-Stampede run; house-right (stage-left) aisle is singled out by forum regulars as the path Young Simba takes, and five rows back is deep enough to appreciate the full stage picture without the Row A neck-crane.

Front-mezz Row A overhangs the orchestra starting at Row P, and on the left/right orchestra the overhang becomes a real distraction behind Row S, but the center orchestra runs deeper before the overhang bites, so Rows P-U down the middle keep a clean view at a significant discount; Row O specifically is flagged as an extra-legroom row. Trade-off: you lose the aisle-procession magic since the parades come down the side aisles.

Minskoff's mezzanine is steeply raked with front-row sections AA-GG that physically extend out over the orchestra, giving Rows A-D center a clean elevated sweep of Pride Rock and the full stage picture aerial puppetry was designed for; the documented trade-off is losing roughly 10 minutes of up-close procession (top and close of each act) that only orchestra-aisle seats deliver, and shorter kids in Row A can be cut off at the bottom by the safety rail (booster seats available).

At 1,710 seats Minskoff is among the larger Broadway houses and the rear mezz amplifies the distance; a recurring patron complaint is that sound goes noticeably lower and can turn muffled, and forum veterans openly call rear-mezz Minskoff 'a barn' where you 'feel like you're sitting in Jersey', with Row L specifically called out as not worth full price (lottery or sub-$60 only).
